output:
Most records you rely on sit with one trusted keeper. Your bank holds the ledger of your account, and you trust it to be honest. A blockchain asks a different question. What if nobody owned the ledger, and everybody held a copy?

That is roughly what it is. A blockchain is a list of transactions, copied across thousands of computers at once. New transactions are bundled into a block, and each block is added to the end of the chain.

The clever part is how the past gets locked in. Every block carries a mathematical fingerprint of the block before it. Change an old entry and that fingerprint breaks, and so does every fingerprint after it. The tampering becomes obvious to everyone holding a copy.

Think of a shared notebook in a room full of people, where each new line references the last. One person scribbling over an old line fools nobody, because everyone else can see the original.

Adding a block takes real effort or a real stake, so dishonesty costs money. That is why no central authority is needed.

It is slow and expensive compared with a bank. It is also very hard to quietly rewrite.

In short, a blockchain is a shared record that everyone can check and nobody can secretly edit.
